paras: The attempted lynching of Amos Miller took place in June 1888 at Franklin, Williamson County, Tennessee, when a mob reported at 75 to 100 men went to the county jail to seize Miller, a Black man about 21 years old accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. Scott, a white woman of Maury County. Officers had taken him out ahead of the mob, which searched the jail, failed to find him and dispersed, and he was taken to Nashville for safekeeping. Papers told the story as one of officers outwitting lynchers, but on August 10, 1888, Miller was taken from the Franklin courtroom and hanged by about fifty armed men.

According to a Nashville dispatch in the Memphis Appeal, the alleged assault took place "Friday, a week ago," and Miller was arrested at Santa Fe, Maury County, and placed in the jail at Columbia. The Atlanta Constitution's Tennessee column, written while he was still at large, placed the crime at Lodebar near the Hickman County line, called the accused "Thomas Davis" and said he was "known also as Amos Miller," and reported that he worked for Scott and that Mrs. Scott was six months pregnant. The same column said that if he were caught "the people will not undergo the expense of taking him to the courthouse for trial." A later roundup reported him jailed at Columbia, where the paper said he had admitted the deed, amid "great excitement."

On a Saturday night the sheriff at Columbia learned that a mob was on its way to the jail and took Miller to Franklin. Sheriff Russell of Williamson County then heard that a mob was bound for Franklin, so he and the jailer hid the prisoner in a wheat field half a mile from town until early morning. The mob reached the jail at about 8 o'clock at night and demanded the prisoner, and according to the Washington Evening Star the turnkey opened the jail and the men searched every cell.

Not finding Miller, the men rode out the Nashville turnpike to the first toll-gate, learned that the sheriff had not passed, and returned to wait around the jail for two hours before dispersing. Meanwhile the jailer took Miller by train from Mallory's Station to Nashville, where he was lodged in jail.

No arrest of anyone in the June mob is reported in the coverage. Miller stayed in Nashville until August 10, when he was brought to Franklin for a special session of court; the mob had promised to let the law take its course if he were tried at once. When his attorneys asked for a continuance, about fifty armed men entered the courtroom, seized him and hanged him from a banister rail almost in the presence of the judge. The Appeal's Franklin correspondent noted that "Several attempts have been made since Miller's arrest to lynch him, but they proved futile until today."

The Memphis Appeal ran the June story on its front page under "How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers," with decks that called the mob "The Assumed Dispensers of Justice" and said they were "Doomed to Defeat." Two days later the Evening Star printed a fuller Nashville telegram headed "To Save a Prisoner from Lynching," which stressed the "hard work" of Tennessee officers. Both papers called Miller "a negro" or "colored" and presented the alleged assault as fact, the Appeal's deck saying he "Assaults a White Lady."

The Atlanta Constitution's weekly Southern roundups went further, calling the case "A horrible crime" and judging it "not improbable that Miller will be lynched." After the August hanging, the Appeal headlined that the story of the crime "Almost Justifies This Disregard for the Law."

The reports disagree on the date of the jail visit: the Appeal's dispatch, dated June 18, put it on the previous night, while the Star's dispatch of June 21 said "Tuesday night," June 19, which cannot be squared with the Appeal's June 19 report. They also differ on when the officers came back from the wheat field (3 or 8 o'clock in the morning) and on the date of the alleged assault.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Amos Miller
bases: A mob of 75-100 men went to the Franklin jail with 'the intention of mobbing' a prisoner accused of assault and searched the cells for him, but he had been removed (A1, A2).

In June the mob of 75-100 failed to find Miller and no one was killed, so this episode was an attempted lynching (A1, A2); Miller was lynched at Franklin on August 10, 1888, which is recorded separately (A6, A7).
Two Nashville dispatches agree on the core attempt, and the Star's adds details the Appeal lacks (A1, A2); the August Appeal confirms that several attempts to lynch Miller had failed (A7).

accounts.label: Nashville dispatch (June 18)
accounts.gist: Officers moved Miller from Columbia to Franklin and hid him in a wheat field; a mob of 75-100 visited the Franklin jail at 8 o'clock 'last night' and dispersed on finding him gone; he was taken to Nashville.

accounts.label: Nashville dispatch (June 21)
accounts.gist: The same story with more detail: the mob entered Franklin 'Tuesday night', the turnkey let it search every cell, it checked the toll-gate on the Nashville turnpike, and dispersed after two hours.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution roundups
accounts.gist: Asserted Miller's guilt, gave the alias Thomas Davis and the place Lodebar, and predicted that he would not get a trial or would likely be lynched.

framing.detail: The Appeal praised the sheriff ('How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers') and mocked the mob as 'The Assumed Dispensers of Justice', while headlining that Miller 'Assaults a White Lady' as fact.
The Evening Star ran the Nashville telegram as 'To Save a Prisoner from Lynching', on the officers' 'hard work'.
The Atlanta Constitution called it 'A horrible crime', said 'the people' would skip a trial, and later called a lynching 'not improbable'.
After the August hanging the Appeal headlined that the story of the crime 'Almost Justifies This Disregard for the Law'.

conflicts.note: The Appeal printed the story in its June 19 issue, so a Tuesday-night (June 19) visit cannot be right for its account; the Star's dispatch reads as a later rewrite with the days shifted. The earlier Tennessee report is the better evidence.
Probably an OCR or transcription difference in the same dispatch.
